summary: Extends IMAP4rev1 to support UTF-8 encoded international characters in user names, mail addresses, and message headers. It is an Experimental protocol and was replaced by RFC 6855.

eli5.summary: Email once handled mostly basic English letters. This extension lets an IMAP mailbox work with names and addresses in many alphabets. It was replaced by RFC 6855.

questions: how does imap support utf-8 usernames
what is the utf8 parameter in imap
how can imap handle international mailbox names
subtitle: Extending IMAP to handle UTF-8 in usernames, mailbox names, and message headers

tldr.problem: IMAP clients and servers only support ASCII in usernames, passwords, mailbox names, and message headers, excluding users with non-ASCII names from using their native credentials and storing messages with international text.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5738 defines new IMAP capabilities (UTF8=ACCEPT, UTF8=USER, UTF8=APPEND, UTF8=ALL, UTF8=ONLY) that allow servers to advertise support for UTF-8, along with rules for up-converting legacy 7-bit mailboxes to UTF-8 when requested.
tldr.outcome: This experimental extension enabled internationalized IMAP usage but was replaced by RFC 6855 with refinements. It was a critical piece enabling the Email Address Internationalization infrastructure.

today: RFC 5738 is Experimental and has been obsoleted by RFC 6855, which refines the specification with additional interoperability guidelines. Systems implementing IMAP internationalization should use RFC 6855 instead of this experimental version.

sections.title: Internationalization in IMAP
sections.content:
IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) is how email clients retrieve messages from servers. RFC 3501 defined IMAP4rev1, but it was restricted to ASCII. This meant users could not:

  • Log in with non-ASCII usernames
  • Use non-ASCII passwords
  • Create or access mailbox names in their native language
  • Receive or view messages with UTF-8 headers

RFC 5738 extends IMAP4rev1 to support UTF-8 in all these areas. It builds on RFC 5335 (internationalized email headers) and works in concert with RFC 5336 and RFC 5504 to provide full internationalization support. The specification defines new capabilities that servers can advertise to indicate what UTF-8 features they support, allowing clients to detect this support and use it appropriately.
sections.eli5: Email inboxes are accessed using a protocol called IMAP. This note updates IMAP to handle non-English letters in login names, passwords, folder names, and message text.

sections.title: UTF-8 IMAP Capabilities
sections.content:
RFC 5738 introduces five new IMAP capabilities, each advertising a different level of UTF-8 support:

  • UTF8=ACCEPT: The server accepts UTF-8 quoted-strings in client commands, supports the UTF8 parameter on SELECT and EXAMINE commands, and returns UTF-8 mailbox names in LIST responses. Clients must use ENABLE to activate this capability.
  • UTF8=USER: The server accepts UTF-8 usernames and passwords in the LOGIN command, applying SASLprep processing for security.
  • UTF8=APPEND: The server accepts UTF-8 headers in messages sent via the APPEND command.
  • UTF8=ALL: All mailboxes on the server support UTF-8. SELECT/EXAMINE with the UTF8 parameter never fail.
  • UTF8=ONLY: The strongest guarantee: the server does not support the legacy modified-UTF-7 mailbox encoding and requires the UTF8 parameter for all mailbox access. This signals a server moving away from backward compatibility.

These capabilities form an implication hierarchy: UTF8=ONLY implies UTF8=ALL, UTF8=APPEND, and UTF8=ACCEPT. UTF8=ALL implies UTF8=ACCEPT.
sections.eli5: Servers can announce different levels of support. A server might handle non-English letters in passwords, or mailbox names, or messages, or all of these. The capabilities tell clients what is available.

sections.title: UTF-8 Quoted Strings
sections.content:
The base IMAP specification requires that 8-bit data be sent as literals (binary blobs), which requires extra round-trips with the server. RFC 5738 introduces UTF-8 quoted strings using a new syntax: asterisk-prefixed strings like *"こんにちは".

When a server advertises UTF8=ACCEPT, clients may use this syntax for any argument that accepts a string, including mailbox names, search criteria, and message content. The server MUST reject octet sequences that violate UTF-8 syntax with a BAD response. Servers MUST NOT send utf8-quoted syntax to clients unless the client has explicitly enabled UTF8=ACCEPT.

This syntax enables more efficient client-server communication when dealing with international characters, avoiding the need for binary literals and their associated delays.
sections.eli5: Instead of sending foreign letters as binary data (which is slow), clients can now send them as quoted text with an asterisk prefix. This is faster and cleaner.

sections.title: The UTF8 SELECT Parameter
sections.content:
When a client executes SELECT or EXAMINE with the UTF8 parameter, the server treats the mailbox as having UTF-8 headers. All IMAP commands related to message sizes, message headers, and MIME body headers return results as if the mailbox were UTF-8 header native.

If a server's mailstore uses 7-bit headers (the legacy format), the server must perform up-conversion when the UTF8 parameter is present. This means decoding RFC 2047-encoded headers, up-converting MIME parameters, decoding IDNA domain names back to Unicode, and expanding other encoded forms to their UTF-8 equivalents.

A server may reject SELECT/EXAMINE with the UTF8 parameter with a [NOT-UTF-8] response code, unless it advertises UTF8=ALL or UTF8=ONLY. Additionally, some mailboxes may require the UTF8 parameter and reject selection without it ([UTF-8-ONLY] response code).
sections.eli5: When opening a folder with the UTF8 option, the server shows messages as if they had non-English letters. Old servers may refuse or may need to convert the stored text.

sections.title: UTF-8 Logins and Mailbox Names
sections.content:
RFC 5738 permits UTF-8 in usernames and passwords when the server advertises UTF8=USER. The LOGIN command arguments are checked against UTF-8 syntax rules from RFC 3629 and validated using SASLprep (RFC 4013) to prevent security issues with lookalike characters.

Mailbox names can contain UTF-8 when the server advertises UTF8=ACCEPT. The RFC mandates that after a client issues 'ENABLE UTF8=ACCEPT', the server MUST NOT return mailbox names in the legacy modified-UTF-7 encoding. Instead, any mailbox with non-ASCII characters MUST be returned using the utf8-quoted syntax.

Mailbox names must comply with the Net-Unicode Definition (allowing all Unicode except control characters and certain separators), ensuring interoperability and consistency across systems.
sections.eli5: Users can now log in with their own names and passwords. Folder names can be in any language. The server keeps track of which encoding format each folder uses.

sections.title: Up-Conversion from Legacy Formats
sections.content:
When a server with 7-bit stored headers permits UTF8 parameter access, it must support up-conversion: converting the stored ASCII-encoded text back to UTF-8 form.

For address headers (From, To, Sender, Cc, Bcc, Reply-To, Resent-From, Resent-To, Resent-Cc, Resent-Bcc), servers must decode:

  • Downgraded addresses (from RFC 5504) to their original UTF-8 form
  • IDNA-encoded domain names (RFC 3490) back to Unicode
  • RFC 2047-encoded display names and comments

For other headers (Subject, Date comments, Comments, Keywords, Content-Description), servers must decode RFC 2047 encoding. At minimum, UTF-8, US-ASCII, and ISO-8859-1 through ISO-8859-15 charsets must be supported, though other charsets may be supported if used elsewhere in IMAP.

Servers SHOULD also up-convert MIME body-part headers and the Content-Disposition filename parameter, but MUST NOT up-convert headers inside multipart/signed (to avoid invalidating signatures) or the Original-Recipient and Return-Path headers (to maintain envelope integrity).
sections.eli5: When an old folder is accessed with UTF8, the server needs to decode all the encoded text back to real letters. This includes email addresses with encoded domains, message subjects, and attachments.
